newsitem.title: PERU: Most of diplomatic hostages now released in Peru.
newsitem.headline: Most of diplomatic hostages now released in Peru.

text.p: At least five ambassadors and four U.S. diplomats were included among Sunday night's release of 225 hostages by Marxist rebels holding the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, Red Cross officials said.

The ambassadors of Bolivia, Guatemala, Panama, Venezuela and the European Union were among the dignitaries named as freed by the Red Cross outside the besieged residence immediately after Tupac Amaru Revolutionary (MRTA) rebels freed the latest group of hostages.
With Sunday's releases, most of the diplomats held in the residence have now been set free.

On the list of releases were the U.S. attaches for economic affairs, drugs and American International Development (AID) plus a more junior American official and the only British diplomat to have been held captive, Roger Church.
The Red Cross named the released Americans as John Riddle, John Crowe, David Bayer and Mike Maxey.
Spain's charge d'affaires, a World Health Organisation official and two United Nations anti-drug officials were also set free.
The guerrillas issued a statement with the released hostages to say they were freeing captives who had no ties to the Peruvian government.

The MRTA said the remaining government-linked hostages included two ministers, vice-ministers, members of the judiciary, legislators, armed forces and police leaders, and representatives of Japanese businesses.
However, Japanese officials in Lima said that at least 10 Japanese nationals were among those freed. They had earlier said that at least 40 -- and possibly as many as 60 -- Japanese were being held.
Additionally, the rebels said they were evaluating the release of some Asian and Latin American diplomats still hostage.
Following Sunday's release of the large group, the rebels still held just over 140 hostages, according to the Red Cross.
